description: Somos un equipo de Quito que trabaja en el desafío Planet X and SPHEREx. Queremos acercar los datos infrarrojos de la misión SPHEREx de la NASA a cualquier persona, convirtiendo unos segundos de atención en una contribución real a la ciencia. Combinamos procesamiento de datos astronómicos, ciencia ciudadana y diseño de experiencias para que explorar el cielo en movimiento sea simple, rápido y accesible para todos.
summary: Sky Task turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a few-second "blink" question anyone can answer: did the circled dot move? A pipeline finds moving objects in SPHEREx images and uses JPL's catalogue of known asteroids as automatic answer keys. An API on Google Cloud serves the tasks to an embeddable  widget that any website or game can add with two lines, and to a public classification page. Answers are stored and weighted by each person's accuracy on known control tasks to build a consensus. It is the blink comparator Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto, brought to where people already spend their time.
details:
What it does: shows a few frames of the same patch of SPHEREx sky blinking, with a ring on one dot, and asks "Moving" or "Not moving". How it works:

  1. Images come from NASA/IPAC IRSA, found with its moving-object search.
  2. Frames are aligned and every source is detected; dots that move in a straight line across 3+ frames are linked.
  3. JPL's Small-Body Identification API labels known asteroids.
  4. Known asteroids (Moving) and stars of similar brightness (Not moving) become control tasks; unexplained candidates become science tasks.
  5. A generator on a home computer keeps producing tasks; a sync script pushes them to Firestore and a private Cloud Storage bucket.
  6. A FastAPI service on Google Cloud Run picks tasks up within a minute and builds a fresh image variant on every request. Each challenge mixes controls with at most 50% unsettled science, and the browser never learns which task is which.
  7. Every answer is saved to Firestore. Votes are weighted by accuracy on controls; a held-out set of controls measures volunteer accuracy honestly. Uses: citizen science (answers recorded; public page at /classify.html), games (a 0–100% score the game turns into its own reward), and, in future, CAPTCHA-style verification. Results: on real SPHEREx data the pipeline recovered 14 of 14 known asteroids blind in their fields, with 0 false tracks; 56+ tasks are live and growing. Nearly every mover SPHEREx can detect is already catalogued, so we present a tested method that carries over to deeper surveys, not a discovery claim. Tools: Python (astropy, astroquery, reproject, sep, numpy, Pillow), FastAPI, Google Cloud Run, Firestore, Cloud Storage, Firebase Hosting, a vanilla-JS web component.
